name: command-with-env-carries-its-entries
note: host::command_with hands the child exactly the environment it is given: FOO reaches the shell, and the parent's own PATH still finds sh, because the executable search happens in the parent.
source: use host;fn main(){mut env=u8[][];env.push("FOO=bar".copy());mut argv=u8[][];argv.push("sh".copy());argv.push("-c".copy());argv.push("echo $FOO".copy());assert(host::command_with(argv,env)==0);}

name: command-with-empty-env-clears-everything
note: An empty environment is the whole environment: `env` prints no variable at all. The shell is not asked, because it would invent a default PATH.
source: use host;fn main(){mut env=u8[][];mut argv=u8[][];argv.push("env".copy());assert(host::command_with(argv,env)==0);}

name: command-with-env-built-from-the-inherited-one
note: host::environment plus one entry is the additive spelling: the child keeps what this process had (PATH) and gains FOO.
source: use host;fn main(){mut env=host::environment();env.push("FOO=bar".copy());mut argv=u8[][];argv.push("sh".copy());argv.push("-c".copy());argv.push("echo $FOO; echo ${PATH+set}".copy());assert(host::command_with(argv,env)==0);}

name: command-without-env-still-inherits
note: The two-argument spelling replaces the environment and nothing else: host::command keeps inheriting this process's, which is why the old call sites did not change.
source: use host;fn main(){mut argv=u8[][];argv.push("sh".copy());argv.push("-c".copy());argv.push("echo ${PATH+inherited}".copy());assert(host::command(argv)==0);}

name: command-with-env-refuses-malformed-entry
note: An entry without = and a non-empty name would make execve start the child with no environment at all (and CreateProcess reject the block), so it is refused with 256+EINVAL and nothing is spawned.
source: use host;fn main(){mut env=u8[][];env.push("NOEQUALS".copy());mut argv=u8[][];argv.push("true".copy());println(host::command_with(argv,env));}

name: command-with-env-reports-a-signalled-child
note: The result convention is shared with host::command: 128+N when signal N ended the child and a normal exit code otherwise, whatever the environment was.
source: use host;fn main(){mut env=u8[][];env.push("X=1".copy());mut argv=u8[][];argv.push("sh".copy());argv.push("-c".copy());argv.push("kill -TERM $$".copy());println(host::command_with(argv,env));}

note: A call-flex hint record names a token span and a locals index of the function that recorded it; token spans are per file. A record left over from the previous file used to index past this function's locals, and hint_use aborted the compiler with SIGABRT and no diagnostic.

name: closure-fnmut-counter
note: A counter closure: the body writes the captured `count`, so the closure is FnMut and calling it takes exclusive access to the closure value; the calls are sequential, so each one sees the previous write.

name: closure-fnmut-disjoint-captures
note: Two FnMut closures over disjoint captures: each writes only its own environment, and holding one exclusively does not block the other.

name: closure-fnmut-sequential-calls
closure-fnmut-second-call-rejected
note: The outer call holds the closure exclusively while its arguments are evaluated, so a call from an argument is a second simultaneous call on the same environment.

name: closure-fnmut-shared-borrow-rejected
note: A shared reference to the closure that is still live (used after the call) blocks the exclusive call. A borrow whose last use has passed is not live, and does not.

name: closure-fnmut-not-fn-rejected
note: FnMut and Fn are different types: a closure that writes a capture cannot be used where a shared call is required, and the diagnostic says why.

name: closure-fnmut-sort-by-counts
note: sort_by takes FnMut: a comparator that counts its calls through a captured `&mut` is accepted, sorts correctly, and the count is visible to the caller afterwards. (A plain captured number is the closure's own copy, so counting into it leaves the caller's binding unchanged; the reference is what reaches the caller.)

name: closure-fn-widens-to-generic-fnmut
note: An Fn closure passed for a generic FnMut(T)->U parameter is widened even when the call learns U from that closure (no type variable is bound yet to widen against); an FnMut closure is accepted the same way.

name: vecs-fnmut-predicates-mutate-captures
note: the predicates and sorters are methods; a mutating FnMut sees exactly the elements a short-circuiting predicate reads

name: vecs-fnmut-predicate-needs-exclusive-capture
note: An FnMut predicate holds its captured `&mut` for as long as the closure lives, so reading the counted binding while the predicate is still to be used is a borrow conflict, not a stale read.

name: pool-join-second-fnmut
note: pool::join's second callback never leaves the calling thread and is called once, so it is FnMut and may write through a captured `&mut`; the first callback crosses to a worker and stays Fn (pool-join-first-fnmut-rejected).

name: pool-join-first-fnmut-rejected
note: pool::join's first callback runs on a worker, so like every pool callback it stays Fn: an FnMut closure there is refused.

name: closure-shared-capture-still-fn
note: A closure that only reads its capture stays Fn: no mutable binding, repeated calls, and it passes where Fn is expected.

name: closure-shared-borrow-of-fn-closure
note: Calling a Fn closure through a live shared reference stays allowed: a shared call does not need the closure exclusively.

name: closure-fnmut-vector-element
note: A FnMut closure over a captured exclusive element reference: each call writes through the captured `&mut u64` and sees the previous value.

name: closure-fnmut-captured-field
note: Writing a field of a captured record stores through an exclusive reference to the environment field.

name: closure-fnmut-needs-mut-binding
closure-fnmut-through-exclusive-reference
note: An adapter takes `&mut FnMut(...)` so it can call the closure exclusively; two calls through the same reference are sequential, so both are allowed.

name: closure-fnmut-mixed-captures
note: Only the capture the body writes is mutable: an untouched capture stays readable, and the closure is FnMut because of the written one.

name: f32-arithmetic-bits
note: Every f32 arithmetic result printed as f64 is its shortest round-trip decimal, so a one-ulp difference anywhere (a widening that is not exact, an operation rounded twice) changes the last digit. The LLVM backend lowers these to fadd/fmul/fdiv float (docs/design/typed-ir.md, F2); the native backend computes in binary64 and rounds once.

name: f32-borrowed-local
note: An f32 local whose address is taken cannot keep its typed-IR fact: the slot is written through a pointer the lifter cannot type, so the fact is dropped and the word lowering stays.

name: parallel-closure-capture-plain-data
note: The closure environment is classified structurally: a record of plain data and a captured shared slice of numbers are both transferable and shareable, so the closure crosses to the workers.

name: pool-chunks-owned
note: A CPU-bound job set: 400k elements summed in 8 owned chunks through pool::split, asserted equal to the sequential answer. The chunk split is one owned vector per job, so no reference crosses a job boundary.

name: pool-map-input-order
note: Job 0 sleeps four times as long as job 3, so completion order is the reverse of input order; pool::map must still return results in input order.

name: pool-uneven-work-no-deadlock
note: One long job (the sum of 0..1999999) among seven trivial ones: no deadlock, and the long job's result lands in its own slot.

name: pool-nested-one-worker
note: Nested parallelism with one worker (GRAIL_WORKERS=1): a job waits on the jobs it forked, so only a waiter that runs its own forks and helps can complete this without deadlock.

name: pool-abort-in-job
note: A job that fails (out-of-bounds) ends the process promptly instead of hanging the pool or its waiter: the failure policy is the runtime's abort policy (B5), and nothing after the abort runs. The abort is raised on a pool worker and surfaces as the abort exit status, exactly like abort-in-green-task-ends-process; an abort raised on the main thread still dies by SIGABRT.

name: pool-speedup-four-workers
note: Wall clock: 3M CPU-bound elements as one job and as four jobs, twice each. Asserts the four-job run is at least 1.5x faster, and SKIPs honestly (stderr only, stdout still "ok") when /proc/cpuinfo reports fewer than four cores. stderr carries the measured times.

name: pool-reject-handle-item
note: The safe pool surface denies a foreign handle: a `handle` has neither Send nor Share, so `pool::map` over handles is refused before any job exists.

name: pool-reject-handle-in-record
note: Structural: a record containing a handle is unshareable too, so it cannot be a pool item. This is the classification the safe surface inherits from parallel_map.

name: pool-from-green-task
note: Parallel work entered from green tasks rather than from the main thread: task_scope resolves the task mode before the pool is ever touched, and two spawned tasks plus the acting task all run owned-chunk jobs. This is the interaction that broke when the task-mode cache and the pool's process-state word were the same word (the pool then 'existed' at address 1 and rt_parallel_map read 0x9), and it is the combination neither branch tested alone.

name: pool-job-handle

name: pool-reject-chunk-alias-vector

diagnostic: use of moved, borrowed or partially initialized value

name: pool-reject-chunk-mutable-capture
note: A chunk callback may not hold an exclusive slice at all: every worker calls the same closure, so a captured &mut [T] would be written by every worker at once. Refused by name, which is the closest a chunk callback gets to writing outside its own region.
diagnostic: cannot share closure capture `w`: a mutable slice or view cannot be shared

name: pool-reject-chunk-shared-slice
note: The in-place surface needs exclusive access, so a shared &[T] is refused rather than handed out as &mut [T].
diagnostic: parallel_split writes through its chunks, so the slice must be exclusive

name: pool-reject-chunk-handle-element
note: The element type goes through the same structural walk as a parallel_map item, so a slice of unaudited handles is refused by name before any job exists - exactly as &[File] is refused as a shared item.
diagnostic: cannot transfer parallel_split element: thread-affine (a foreign handle with no audited classification)

name: pool-reject-chunk-handle-capture
note: The closure environment is classified for chunks exactly as for parallel_map: a handle captured by the callback reaches a thread-affine resource from every worker.
diagnostic: cannot share closure capture `f`: f is thread-affine (a foreign handle with no audited classification)

name: pool-reject-chunk-fnmut-capture
note: An FnMut closure shared by every worker would race on its own environment, the same refusal parallel_map gives.
diagnostic: a callback shared by concurrent workers must not write a captured value

name: pool-chunk-write-outside-aborts
note: The runtime half of 'a chunk cannot write outside itself': the slice a callback holds has its own length, so an index at or past that length is a bounds abort rather than a write into a sibling chunk. Nothing after the abort runs.

name: pool-reject-job-borrowed-capture
note: A job handle outlives the statement that spawned it, and a Job<R>'s type records no lifetime, so a callback that captured a borrow could carry it out of the frame it points into: refused instead of silently made unsound.
diagnostic: a job handle may outlive this statement, so its callback cannot capture a borrow

name: pool-reject-job-of-job
note: A job cannot return a handle: two waits on one record would free it twice.
diagnostic: a pool job cannot return a Task or Job handle

name: pool-reject-job-double-join
note: A handle is move-only: the wait consumes it, so the record is freed exactly once and no second wait can exist.
diagnostic: use of moved, borrowed or partially initialized value

name: pool-reject-job-in-map
note: A handle cannot cross another job boundary as an item or a result: it is a must-wait value with one owner.
diagnostic: parallel_map cannot move Task or job handles between threads

name: pool-reject-job-borrowed-closure
note: A job owns its closure: it drops the environment on the worker that ran it. A closure passed by reference is still dropped by its owner, so taking it would free one object twice - refused rather than left to the caller's drop.
diagnostic: a pool job takes its closure by value

name: task-100k-spawn-join-checksum

name: task-fib-spreads-across-workers
note: A fork-join over fib-sized work records the worker id of every task; a start barrier forces two tasks to run at once, which requires two workers, so more than one worker id must be seen whenever the scheduler has more than one worker. On a single-worker/thread mode the assertion degrades to 'at least one id'.

name: task-sleep-timers-overlap
note: Green tasks sleep on the platform timer and wake in parallel: eight 30 ms sleeps finish in far less than the serial 240 ms.

name: task-steal-stress-tree
note: A four-level fork-join tree spawned from stolen tasks: 2048 leaves cross the deques, so a lost or doubled push/pop/steal changes the checksum.

name: pool-abort-eight-chunks-reports-once
note: Eight parallel chunks write one past their own slice at once. The abort is reported exactly once and the process exits 134 instead of dying by SIGABRT from a second reporter.

name: main-stack-overflow-reports-and-exits-134
note: Recursion on the main thread runs the kernel's stack out. There is no page the runtime can make PROT_NONE there, so the fault is recognised by its distance from the interrupted stack pointer (read out of ucontext) and reported on the alternate stack: the same message a task's overflow prints, the statement the frame was entering, and status 134. The fault lands in a frame's prologue, whose statement entry carries no position, so the location is the first statement of the function that overflowed. On every backend: the location line is pinned by main-stack-overflow-names-the-place, native only.

name: main-stack-overflow-names-the-place
note: the report names where the stack ran out; the location comes from the site table, which only the native backend emits (the LLVM path has none: docs/testing.md)

name: wild-pointer-dies-by-sigsegv-without-an-overflow-report
note: The stack-fault handler must not swallow a real memory fault: a null dereference is far from the stack pointer, so the handler restores the default disposition and the process dies of SIGSEGV with nothing on stderr. Needs libc, so it runs on x86_64 only (the cross targets link without one).

name: deep-recursion-that-ends-is-unaffected

name: task-stack-overflow-reports-and-exits-134
note: A task recurses past the bottom of its 1 MiB stack into the PROT_NONE guard page: the alternate-stack fault handler names the overflow and exits 134, and the program never reaches its join.

name: bce-for-len-read-write
